newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Illegal imports threaten Yugo tobacco industry.
newsitem.headline: Illegal imports threaten Yugo tobacco industry.

text.p: Yugoslavia's tobacco industry faces closures unless the government clamps down on booming illegal cigarette trade, accounting for 90 percent of domestic consumption, industry officials warned on Thursday.

"We want the state to put an end to cigarette smuggling, to block any imports of goods we produce, to abide by the laws it has adopted and prepare a programme for this industry," general manager of the Duvanska Industrija Nis (DIN) Smiljko Kostic said.
Warnings came after the industry sold only 202 tonnes of home produced cigarettes in March or 10 percent of the total monthly consumption estimated at around 2,000 tonnes.
"Those were the lowest monthly sales in the history of our industry," said Svetozar Zlatkovic, director of the Yugoslav Tobacco Fund.
Smuggled cigarettes accounted for 71 percent of local consumption in 1996.
"We want the finance ministry, police and the army to join the fight against cigarette smuggling," Kostic said.
Despite frequent pledges to clamp down on illegal cigarette imports the government has done little so far, leading industry analysts to think the state had a "cut" in the business.
Industry officials called on the state to burn all seized cigarettes, ban street trade and provide more financial help.
"Our time is running out and the state must do something if it wants the industry to work at full capacities," said Slavoljub Vuckovic of the Duvanska Industrija Vranje (DIV).
"We do not want to create any problems, but if no measures are taken we have no other choice but to stop production, send people home and the consequences will be immense," he said.
If the state takes no action it will face a wave of workers' unrest, industry sources said.

"We urgently need to see what the state plans to do with us. If not, it will no longer talk to us directors but to workers. We can no longer control trade unions. They expect an answer from us by Tuesday," Kostic said.
In the absence of state help cigarette producers were only making losses, Kostic added.

"This industry can bring the state around three billion dollars, one billion at once through development programmes. But if there is no help, we'll close down and no local bank will ever be able to finance revival of the industry," he said.
Director of the largest Yugoslav tobacco plant said DIN may seek permission from the state to locate its production capacities outside Yugoslavia if no action is taken.
"We'll go to Russia, produce there and we'll succeed because we are good at this. We are only not good at regulating smuggling business," Kostic added.
Tobacco producers said declining output led to further deterioration of production capacities and created enormous illiquidity in the sector.

Low sales brought practically no money to state coffers even though more than half of the price of domestic cigarettes flows into them. The state takes 40 percent in excise duties and another 23 percent from the sales tax.

"The state tolerates its losses, but it should let us live and work properly. The state should free us from those taxes. This will make our cigarettes cheaper because we shall sell at producer prices," Vuckovic said.

Producers said the state had to legalise cigarette imports. They also wanted all credits given to tobacco producers from the central bank to be rescheduled for five years and some short-term commercial credits to be swapped for equity.

Yugoslav tobacco producers need around 70 million dinars ($12.38 million) for its 1997 crop, another 40 million dinars to build 2,000 dryer plants and 35 million dinars a year for research and development.
Funds can be secured if prices go up by 0.5 dinars per cigarette pack, but only if that money is not subject to taxes and is paid directly to the Tobacco Fund.

Yugoslavia produced 4,200 tonnes of raw tobacco in 1996. For the current year, cigarette producers estimate their total needs at 17,365 tonnes of various sorts of tobacco. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
($1 = 5.6506 Yugoslav dinars)
